abstract.p: In this study, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, a hybrid material, capable of absorbing visible light, was designed and synthesized easily through growth of COF-MT by imine bond formation using amine groups of supported melamine on γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2. The structure, morphology and optical properties of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT were investigated using various techniques, including FT-IR, UV-vis DRS, PXRD, TGA, XPS, FESEM, EDS mapping, TEM, VSM, BET, BJH, PL, ICP, EIS and Mott-Schottky plots. This hybrid material was effectively utilized as a ternary heterostructure photocatalyst to achieve efficient and selective oxidation of alcohols into aldehydes under sunlight irradiation and air bubbling in ethanol. The remarkably improved photocatalytic performance is attributed to enhanced charge separation, increased visible light absorption, and the strengthened redox capabilities of photogenerated electrons and holes through a dual S-scheme charge transfer mechanism. Based on our knowledge, this is the first report on the photo-oxidation of alcohols catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MOF/COF as a hybrid material. This work highlights the potential of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT as a sustainable catalyst for the synthesis of aldehydes as fine chemicals due to the improved light absorption and charge separation, energy-saving (sunlight irradiation), mild reaction conditions (room temperature and ambient pressure), using a small amount of the catalyst, air as a safe and plentiful oxidant (generating water as the only by-product), ethanol as a green solvent, and the ease of catalyst isolation and reuse by an external magnet without a remarkable change in the catalyst structure and activity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, the development of novel heterogeneous photocatalysts for converting solar energy into practical energy sources has garnered significant global interest in response to climate change and the energy shortage1. Photocatalytic organic transformations hold great promise for fine chemical synthesis, because of their sustainable nature, mild reaction conditions, and the potential utilization of solar energy. There is a large variety of chemical reactions well catalyzed by heterogeneous photocatalysts. However, there is a challenge in using a pure semiconducting material as an efficient photocatalyst due to the high recombination rate of electronic-hole pairs and the limitation in the harvest of visible light. One way to overcome this limitation is the design of heterojunctions by combining of two or more different semiconductors with proper band gap alignments. In the obtaining heterostructure materials, the electron and hole pairs were separated sufficiently to decrease the recombination rate and enhance the photocatalytic activity. Amongst different electron-hole transfer pathways, S-scheme heterojunction has been known as the most efficient strategies to advance the photocatalytic activity2–4. This charge transfer mechanism effectively enhances the charge carrier separation, preventing the photocarrier recombination rate, and preserving high redox capacity. In S-scheme photocatalysts, electrons move from the conduction band of one semiconductor to the valence band of the other semiconductor due to the internal electric field at the interface between the two semiconductors. This creates an S-shaped electron migration path. Therefore, electrons and holes that have a strong redox potential are preserved, and those with a weaker redox potential are transferred and consumed.

It is well known that the development of a simple way to recycle a photocatalyst can prevent excessive use of photocatalysts, and decrease the overall expense. Over the years, incorporating of the nanomagnetic materials with semiconductors to produce a heterostructure of nanomagnetic/semiconductor has become an easy and comfortable technique for the catalyst separation and reuse5,6. In iron oxide/semiconductor composites, iron oxide offers benefits including low cost, high stability, and excellent compatibility. It facilitates the straightforward separation of the photocatalyst from the solution while also contributing synergistically to the photocatalytic efficiencies of the composite as a semiconductor7.

In recent years, among various heterogeneous photocatalysts, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as new classes of semiconductors for photocatalysis due to their distinctive characteristics8–10. MOFs are constructed by the self-assembly of metal ions/clusters and organic ligands through coordination bonds, and COFs are composed of organic ligands containing light elements, combined through covalent bonds11. They are porous crystalline frameworks with high specific surface area, uniform but tunable pore sizes, extendable adsorption spectrum, and clear structural regularity12,13. The porous structure and surface properties of MOFs and COFs can be easily optimized through monomer design at the molecular level or through post synthetic modification of the synthesized skeletons. The adjustability of MOFs and COFs gives the more structural optimization possibilities. However, in spite of outstanding inherent properties of MOFs and COFs, there is a limitation in their photocatalytic applications owing to their low charge separation performances and fast recombination of photo-generated charge carriers. The construction of heterojunctions such as a MOF/COF hybrid with band gap alignments is an efficient approach to enhance the lifetime of photo-induced charge carriers and visible-light harvesting region through the upgraded conjugated system14,15. Moreover, the integration of MOFs and COFs preserves the advantages of both components while generating a synergistic effect that imparts multifunctional properties, addresses their inherent limitations, and enhances the catalytic performance and stability beyond that of the individual materials. MOF/COF hybrid materials mostly prepared through covalent bond formations (e.g. imine, amide and coordination bonds), or non-covalent formations such as π-π stacking interaction16,17. Covalent bond formation is more advantageous than other types of connections, due to both stablished combination and movement of photo-generated charge carriers. Particularly, MOFs are applied for growing COFs largely via an imine bond formation between the aldehyde monomers of COFs and the reserved –NH2 groups of MOFs to make MOF/COF hybrid materials10,18,19. COFs with high stability can provide stronger protection for the hybrid material. MOF/COF hybrid materials are utilized in various fields such as catalysis, gas adsorption, sensing, energy storage, and photodynamic therapy15,20–23. They have shown high photocatalytic activity in different reactions such as hydrogen evolution, CO2 reduction, H2O2 production, degradation, cross-coupling reactions, reduction of 4-nitrophenol, and styrene oxidation8–10,19,24–26. However, less research has been concerned on improving their ease of separation by making nanomagnetic iron oxide/MOF/COF hybrid materials27–29. Notably, the improvement of photocatalytic activity of MOF/COF hybrid materials by the synergistic contribution of nanomagnetic iron oxide as a semiconductor is missed.

Aldehyde or ketone derivatives were employed mainly as fine chemicals and precursors to produce diverse drugs, fragrances, vitamins, dyes, rubbers, polymers, resins and spices30–35. Selective oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes or ketones, ranks among the most extensively studied chemical processes in both chemical laboratory and industry36,37. Traditional synthetic processes for the oxidation of alcohols, often employed stoichiometric amounts of aggressive oxidants, e.g. MnO4−, Cr2O72−, Br2 and ClO-38–40. These methods unavoidably produce harmful wastes during simultaneous reduction of the oxidants, which are undesirable from environmental and pharmaceutical viewpoints. They also exhibit low selectivity toward desired valuable chemicals as a result of the harsh reaction conditions typically employed41. Whereas, thermo-catalytic alcohol oxidations mediated by oxidants such as H2O2, molecular oxygen and air can effectively avoid these disadvantages and treat as environmentally friendly oxidants42–44. During these oxidation methods, the oxidants are reduced to water as the only by-product. Nevertheless, thermo-catalytic methods frequently demand harsh temperature and/or pressure conditions, which result in the production of unwanted by-products, reduce atom efficiency, posing considerable environmental and safety issues. Compared with thermo-catalytic oxidation, photocatalytic approaches, specially under visible light, are promising alternative routes due to the advantages of mild reaction conditions (room temperature and ambient pressure), energy-saving (using cheap and clean renewable solar energy), environmental friendliness, and sustainability45–48. Although numerous heterogeneous photocatalysts have been introduced for the synthesis of aldehydes from alcohols using oxygen as an oxidizing agent,45–48 to date, only a single study has reported the use of a hybrid of MOF and COF as a photocatalyst for this transformation9. However, the practical use of this method is restricted by certain limitations such as long reaction time (30 h), requiring a large amount of the catalyst (100 mg for 1 mmol alcohol), lack of using a green solvent and difficulty in catalyst isolation (centrifuging is required). In fact, there is a plenty of room to explore the unfulfilled capabilities of MOF/COF hybrid materials as effective novel photocatalysts for the synthesis of aldehydes as fine chemicals.

Following up our recent contributions dealing with developing new photocatalysts for the organic transformations49–52, in this work, a novel nanomagnetic iron oxide/MOF/COF hybrid material denoted as γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was successfully constructed. For this purpose, initially, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 was synthesized and modified with melamine for further growth of COF on the MOF. Amine groups of supported melamine on magnetic MOF contribute to produce COF through imine bond formation between terephthalaldehyde and nitrogen-containing monomers (melamine). γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was successfully applied as a dual S-scheme ternary heterostructure for the efficient and selective oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes under sunlight irradiation by air as an abundant oxidant in ethanol as a green solvent. Based on our knowledge, this represents the first reported instance of photo-oxidation of alcohols catalyzed by a nanomagnetically separable MOF/COF hybrid material.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: Chemicals were sourced from the Merck Chemical Company. Product purity and reaction progress were monitored using thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on silica-gel polygram SILG/UV254 plates. FT-IR spectra were obtained using a Shimadzu Fourier Transform infrared spectrophotometer (FT-IR-8300). Diffuse Reflectance Spectroscopy (DRS) was carried via a Japan UV-VIS analyzer (Model V-670). X-ray diffractometer (X’Pert PRO, PANalytical, Netherlands) was used to record XRD patterns. Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed on a Shimadzu thermogravimetric analyzer (TG-50). XPS analyses were conducted with a XPS Nexsa from ThermoFisher Scientific and a VG-Microtech Multilab 3000 spectrometer equipped with an Al anode, and spectral deconvolution was performed using Gaussian–Lorentzian curves. FE-SEM and Energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS) mapping was carried out with a MIRA3TESCAN-XMU. TEM analysis was conducted using an American Ziess EM900 microscope and vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) survey was performed via American VSM analyzer model 7407, which manufactured by Lake Shore Cryotronics. Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) and pore size analysis (BJH analysis) were conducted by nitrogen adsorption on a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 (USA) and a Fisisorción-3 3Flex from Micromeritics. A RF-5301 series instrument model Shimadzu performed photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy [excited at λ = 358 nm]. An Autolab PGSTAT302 potentiostate with a FRA32M module (Metrohm) was employed for electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Mott–Schottky analysis were done on a µStat-i 400 s (Metrohm DropSens) portable potentiostat/galvanostat/impedance analyzer. Varian (730-ES) ICP analyzer determined the metal (Fe) content on the catalyst. Karmana photonics manufactured by Kerman Science and Technology Park (Iran) was employed as solar simulator.

sec.title: Synthesis of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2
sec.p: γ-Fe2O353 (0.06 g) was sonicated in dimethylformamide (12 mL) for 30 min at room temperature. FeCl3·6H2O (2.01 g) as a metal node and 2-aminoterephthalic acid as a ligand (0.66 g) were separately dissolved in dimethylformamide (22 mL) and mixed together. Then this mixture was gradually added to the sonicated γ-Fe2O3 in DMF. The mixture was stirred for one hour at room temperature, then placed inside an autoclave at 110 ℃ for 24 h. The resulting precipitate was separated using an external magnet, washed with dimethylformamide (3 × 20 mL) and ethanol (3 × 20 mL), and dried in an oven at 80 ℃ for 24 h.

sec.title: Synthesis of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL
sec.p: The synthesized γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (0.5 g) from the previous step was dispersed in dry tetrahydrofuran (40 mL) and sonicated for 30 min. The reaction vessel was then cooled in an ice bath, and a solution of cyanuric chloride (0.4 g) in dry THF (10 mL) was added. It was stirred for 14 h in the ice bath and then for an additional 20 h at room temperature. A solution of ammonia (0.5 mL, 25%) was added dropwise to the reaction vessel and stirred at room temperature for 30 min. The mixture was finally refluxed for 12 h under argon atmosphere. The resulting precipitate was isolated, washed with dimethyl sulfoxide (3 × 20) and EtOH (3 × 15), and then dried in an oven at 80 ℃ for 24 h.

sec.title: Synthesis of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT
sec.p: The as-prepared γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL (0.2 g) was sonicated in dry DMSO (10 mL) for approximately 30 min. Solutions of terephthalaldehyde (0.5 g) in DMSO (5 mL) and melamine (0.5 g) in DMSO (5 mL) was added to the dispersed mixture, which was then placed in an autoclave at 180 ℃ for 12 h. After cooling to room temperature, the resulting solid was collected using an external magnet, washed with DMSO (3 × 15 mL) and ethanol (3 × 10 mL), and finally dried in an oven at 80 ℃ for 24 h. The iron content of the produced γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was quantified by ICP analysis indicating 0.45 mmol of Fe per 1 g of it.

sec.title: Synthesis of COF-MT
sec.p: A solution of melamine (0.5 g in 5 mL DMSO) was added to terephthalaldehyde (0.5 g in 5 mL DMSO), and placed in a 100 mL autoclave at 180 ℃ for 12 h. The resulting precipitate was separated by centrifugation and washed with dry DMSO (3 × 10 mL) and ethanol (3 × 10 mL). Finally, the product was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 ℃ for 24 h.

sec.title: General procedure for the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohols to benzaldehydes catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT
sec.p: γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (0.005 g) was added to a solution of alcohol (1 mmol) in ethanol (3 mL). The reaction mixture was stirred under sunlight (using a solar simulator) and air bubbling at 27 ℃. The progress of the reaction was monitored using TLC. After a suitable time (Table 2), the catalyst was isolated using an external magnet, washed with ethanol (2 × 5 mL), and reused for a new identical process. Pure products were obtained by evaporating the remaining solvent and performing chromatography on silica gel using n-hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent with a ratio of 10:2.

sec.title: Synthesis of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT
sec.p: γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was synthesized as shown in Fig. 1. At first, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 was synthesized from γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles, 2-aminoterephthalic acid, and FeCl3·6H2O by a modified solvothermal method at 110 ℃ in DMF52,54. The as-prepared magnetic MOF was then reacted with cyanuric chloride and subsequently with NH3 to produce supported melamine on magnetic MOF [γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL]. Finally, amine groups of supported melamine on magnetic MOF contribute to growth COF-MT (melamine-terephthalaldehyde) through imine bond formation between terephthalaldehyde and melamine as a nitrogen-containing monomers.

caption.p: Synthetic route for the preparation of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: The synthesized γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was characterized by a variety of techniques such as FT-IR, UV-vis DRS, PXRD, TGA, XPS, FESEM, EDS mapping, TEM, VSM, BET, BJH, PL, ICP, EIS and Mott-Schottky plots.

FT-IR spectra of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are presented in Fig. 2. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, peaks at 577 and 525 cm− 1 were related to Fe–O bond vibration. The bands at approximately 1500–1670 and 1290–1434 cm− 1 were assigned to the C = O and C = C stretching vibrations in γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2. A peak at 1223–1261 cm− 1 was ascribed to C-N bond vibration. After hybrid formation, some new broad peaks appeared in the FT-IR spectrum of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT at around 1553, 1482 and 1351 cm− 1 (Fig. 2b) corresponding to C = N, C = C and C-N bonds, respectively.

caption.p: FT-IR spectra of (a) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and (b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: UV–vis DRS spectrum of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT exhibits a broad absorption band in the visible light region (380–850 nm) and a remarkable lowering in the band gap energy compared with γ-Fe2O3, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL and COF-MT (Figs. 3 and 4). These findings primarily result from the increased conjugation across the hybrid structure in γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT, which facilitates more efficient electron delocalization and consequently lowers the band gap energy between the valence and conduction bands.

caption.p: UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra of γ-Fe2O3, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.
Tauc plots of (a) γ-Fe2O3, (b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, (c) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, (d) COF-MT, and (e) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed for γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 5). As shown in Fig. 5d, in the XRD pattern of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, three identified diffraction peaks at 9.0, 10.4 and 18.7° were observed for MIL101(Fe)-NH2, which are matching with the simulated XRD pattern of MIL101(Fe) (Fig. 5b)50,55. These peaks were also observed in the XRD pattern of the synthesized MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (Fig. 5c). Moreover, in Fig. 5d, peaks at 2θ = 30.0, 35.6, 43.3, 53.9, 57.4, and 63.0° were related to the (220), (311), (400), (422), (511), and (440) reflections of cubic maghemite56. The observed peaks are consistent with those of the synthesized γ-Fe2O3 (Fig. 5a). The presence of the peaks of MOF and iron oxide in the XRD pattern of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT showed preservation of the structure of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe) in these compounds (Fig. 5e, g). A broad diffraction peak at 14–27° in Fig. 5g could confirm the successful composite formation of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL with COF-MT. As shown in the XRD pattern of COF-MT (Fig. 5f), this broad peak is the characteristic peak of COF-MT. The broad diffraction features observed for COF-MT originates from its intrinsically low crystallinity and are consistent with previously reported patterns57,58.

caption.p: XRD patterns of (a) γ-Fe2O3, (b)MIL101(Fe)-Simulated, (c) MIL101(Fe)-NH2, (d) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, (e) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, (f) COF-MT, and (d) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: Thermogravimetric (TG) and differential thermogravimetric (DTG) analyses investigated the thermal degradation behavior of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 6). The TG-DTG curves showed that these species exhibited similar weight loss patterns. As shown in Fig. 6a, TG-DTG analysis of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT showed an initial weight loss of 6% (from 25 to 140 ℃) owing to the solvent release, followed by a weight loss of about 78% at 300 to 555 ℃ due to the thermal degradation of organic counterparts in γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT. Appearing of the second weight loss at higher temperature compared with γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (Fig. 6b) and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL (Fig. 6c), indicated the higher thermal stability of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, which can be a result of MOF modification with COF-MT.

caption.p: TG-DTG analysis of (a) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, (b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, and (c) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL.

sec.p: XPS analysis was done to depict the chemical composition of the surfaces of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, COF-MT, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, γ-Fe2O3, and MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (Fig. 7). The observed peaks in the XPS elemental survey of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 7a), are corresponded to carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Two peaks related to carbon and nitrogen in the XPS of COF-MT (Fig. 7b) and four peaks related to oxygen, iron, carbon and nitrogen, were observed in the XPS of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL (Fig. 7c). Two peaks related to oxygen and iron, were observed in the XPS of γ-Fe2O3 (Fig. 7d). Four peaks related to carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and iron, were observed in the XPS of MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (Fig. 7e). XPS analysis is sensitive to the outermost layers of a material (typically 1–10 nanometers). An increase in the atomic ratio of the carbon and nitrogen to the oxygen in γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, compared with γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL (Table 1S), indicates that COF-MT is hybridized with γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL. C1s spectrum (Fig. 7f) of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT showed binding energies at 284.6 (Csp2–N, C–C and C = C), 286.4 (C–O), 287.5 (C = N), and 288.5 (C = O) eV26,27,59,60. Peaks at 398.2 and 399.4 eV in the N1s spectrum (Fig. 7g) are assigned to the C − N and C = N bonds, respectively61. O1s XPS spectrum (Fig. 7h) displays peaks with the binding energies of 530.9, 532.3, and 533.7 eV, which are ascribed to the Fe − O, C = O, and O = C–O bonds, respectively10,59,62. Deconvoluted XPS spectra of C1s and N1s of COF-MT, C1s, N1s and O1s of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, O1s and Fe2p of γ-Fe2O3, and C1s, N1s, O1s and Fe2p of MIL101(Fe)-NH2 are presented in the supporting information (Figs. 1S, 2S, 3S and 4S).

caption.p: XPS analysis of (a) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (b) COF-MT, (c) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, (d) γ-Fe2O3 and (e) MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and deconvoluted XPS spectra of (f) C1s, (g) N1s and (h) O1s of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: FE-SEM images of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are presented in Fig. 8a-e. FE-SEM images of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂ (Fig. 8a, b) revealed that MOF building blocks exhibit a well-defined, uniform octahedral morphology with sharp corners. The edge length of the octahedron is approximately 500–800 nm. Figure 8c-e clearly revealed the presence of MOF and COF in the MOF/COF hybrid material. The morphology of MOF remains intact after hybrid formation. Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) indicated the uniform elemental composition of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and iron in the elemental mapping of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 8f-j).

caption.p: FE-SEM images of (a, b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂, (c-e) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT, and EDS mapping images of (f) carbon, (g) nitrogen, (h) oxygen, (i) iron, and (j) carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and iron in γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT.

sec.p: Transmission electron microscopic (TEM) images of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are presented in Fig. 9. A well-defined regular octahedral structure of MOF with the edge length of around 500–800 nm and spherical γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles were detected in the TEM image of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 (Fig. 9a). Figure 9b revealed that units of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 were incorporated into the COF-MT as the organic layer, with the thickness of about 50–100 nm.

caption.p: TEM images of (a) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and (b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: A vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) was used to characterize the magnetic properties of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 10). The saturation magnetization values for γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are 32.4, 26.1 and 16.5 emu.g− 1, respectively. Despite of the presence of COF-MT layers on the surface of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, the final product maintains its strong saturation magnetization, making it suitable for separation and recovery with an external magnet.

caption.p: VSM analysis of (a) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, (b) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, and (c) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms for γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Figs. 5S and 11) revealed Type IV profiles with H3 hysteresis loops for these materials10. An increase in the surface area from 114.21 for γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2 to 351.41 for γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-MEL and finally to 760.89 m²·g⁻¹ for γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT through successive modifications, correlating with an increase in the N2 uptake capacity, demonstrated the pore development during hybrid formation. BJH pore size distribution analysis revealed pores diameter distributions of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was specified at 5.9 nm, confirming the mesoporous structure of this composite (Fig. 11).

sec.p: PL emission spectra of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT were studied to determine the separation of electron-hole pairs and charge transfer in these compounds (Fig. 12). The intensity of PL spectrum of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT compared with those of MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and COF-MT is obviously decreased. Weaker PL intensity of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT represented the efficient separation and the higher lifetime of the photogenerated electron-hole pairs with a lower recombination rate, resulting in better photocatalytic efficiency.

sec.title: Photo-oxidation of alcohols catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT
sec.p: After full characterization of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, the photocatalytic performance of this material was investigated in the alcohol oxidation. For this purpose, benzyl alcohol was selected as a model alcohol to evaluate the catalytic performance of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT under various conditions (Table 1). Reaction of the model alcohol was studied using different amounts of the catalyst, various solvents, lighting sources and oxidizing agents. The highest yield of benzaldehyde (1 mmol) was achieved using 0.005 g of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT as the catalyst, activated by sunlight irradiation with air as the oxidizing agent in EtOH (Table 1, entry 3). Without the catalyst or when conducted under a nitrogen atmosphere, no product was formed (Table 1, entries 1 and 14). Under dark conditions or with alternative oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide and t-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP), the yield of benzaldehyde was not high (Table 1, entries 11, 15 and 16).

caption.p: Photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT in different conditions.

table-wrap-foot.p: a Reaction conditions: benzyl alcohol (1 mmol), solvent (3 mL), γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT as catalyst (except in entry 1), at 27 ℃, under air bubbling as oxidant (except in entries 14–16), and simulated sunlight irradiation (except in entries 12 and 13). b Under dark conditions, c blue-LED visible light irradiation, d room light. e N2 atmosphere. f TBHP and g H2O2 as oxidizing agent (1 mmol).

sec.p: Following the examination of optimal reaction conditions for the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, the applicability of this method for the oxidation of different alcohols was explored. The results are depicted in Table 2.

As indicated in Table 2, different types of substituted benzyl alcohols with electron-withdrawing or electron-releasing groups were selectively oxidized to their corresponding aldehydes (Entries 1–8). Additionally, cinnamyl alcohol as an α,β-unsaturated alcohol, furfuryl alcohol as a heterocyclic alcohol, and aliphatic alcohols were selectively oxidized to the desired products, under the optimized reaction conditions (Table 2, entries 9–13).
Structural characterization of the reaction products was performed using1H and13C NMR spectroscopy. 1H and13C NMR spectra of the products are shown in the Supporting Information (Figs. 6–19 S).

caption.p: Photo-oxidation of alcohols catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT under sunlight irradiation with air in EtOH.a.

table-wrap-foot.p: a Reaction conditions: alcohol (1 mmol), EtOH (3 mL), catalyst (0.005 g), 27 ℃, air bubbling and simulated sunlight irradiation.

sec.p: Heterogeneous nature of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was investigated through hot filtration test for the model reaction under optimized conditions. In the hot filtration test, after approximately 40% conversion of benzyl alcohol (Fig. 13a), the solid was separated using an external magnetic field (Fig. 13b) and stirred at room temperature for 8 h. Any further transformation was not detected (Fig. 13c), which was indicated the heterogeneity of the catalyst. The reusability and stability of heterogeneous catalysts is crucial from both environmental and practical perspectives. Therefore, the reusability of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was examined in the oxidation reaction of benzyl alcohol under optimized reaction conditions. The catalytic activity of the recovered catalyst remained consistent after seven runs (Fig. 13d). XRD, FT-IR, and XPS analyses of both fresh and recovered γ-Fe2O3/MIL-101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT after seven catalytic cycles confirmed the preservation of the catalyst structural integrity and crystallinity (Fig. 13e–h). FE-SEM and TEM images of the reused catalyst showed a high degree of similarity to those of the fresh sample, indicating that the catalyst morphology preserved well after seven cycles (Fig. 13i-l). In addition, the leaching behavior of the catalyst components was evaluated by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis, which revealed negligible iron release into the solution (< 0.1%). This minimal leaching demonstrates the high stability of the photocatalyst and suggests a low risk of environmental impact. In overall, these findings confirm the excellent structural stability and reusability of γ-Fe2O3/MIL-101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT.

caption.p: (a) Dispersion of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT in ethanol, (b) Isolation of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT by an external magnetic field, (c) Hot filtration test, (d) Reusability, (e) XRD pattern and (f) FT-IR spectra of the fresh and reused catalyst, XPS spectra of (g) the fresh and (h) reused catalyst, FE-SEM images of (i) the fresh and (j) reused catalyst, and TEM images of (k) the fresh and (l) reused catalyst.

sec.p: Photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol in the presence of 1,4-benzoquinone and ammonium oxalate, as the scavengers of superoxide radicals (O₂•−) and photogenerated holes (h+), respectively, under optimized reaction conditions were studied (Table 3). As it is evidenced in Table 3, significant reductions in the photo-oxidation efficiency in the presence of these scavengers is a good indication that the main active species in this photocatalytic system are O₂•− and h+.

sec.p: Photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde was investigated in the presence of COF-MT and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂ under optimized reaction conditions. The findings of this study were compared with that of γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT as a MOF-COF hybrid material (Fig. 14). As indicated in Fig. 14, γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂/COF-MT showed enhanced catalytic activity compared to its precursors. The greater catalytic activity is likely due to the synergistic effect of the hybrid precursors.

caption.p: Photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde in the presence of COF-MT and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH₂ compared with γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT. Reaction conditions: benzyl alcohol (1 mmol), EtOH (3 mL), catalyst (0.005 g), under air bubbling, at 27 ℃, 9 h.

sec.p: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) diagrams of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are shown in Fig. 15. The iron oxide/MOF/COF hybrid material exhibits a smaller charge transfer resistance. These results showed that the heterojunction structure facilitates rapid migration of photogenerated charge carriers, due to the synergistic interfacial effects.

caption.p: EIS diagrams of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT.

sec.p: Mott-Schottky plots of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are shown in Fig. 16a-d. Positive slopes of Mott-Schottky curves indicate that γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT are n-type semiconductors. The flat-band potentials (Efb) of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, COF-MT, and γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT were determined to be + 0.16, + 0.68, −0.91, and + 0.46 eV vs. Ag/AgCl, and + 0.36, + 0.88, −0.71 and + 0.66 eV vs. normal hydrogen electrode (NHE), respectively (ENHE =EAg/AgCl + 0.197)63. Using the obtained flat-band potentials and the measured optical band gaps (Fig. 4), the valence band potentials (EVB) of γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2, and COF-MT were estimated to be + 2.36, + 3.08, and + 1.59 eV vs. NHE (Fig. 16e).

caption.p: Mott-Schottky plots of (a) γ-Fe2O3, (b) MIL101(Fe)-NH2, (c) COF-MT, and (d) γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT, and (e) energies of MIL101(Fe)-NH2, γ-Fe2O3, and COF-MT.

sec.p: Based on our findings and the reported mechanisms in the literature4,64, two charge transfer mechanisms (type II and dual S-scheme) can be proposed for the photo-oxidation of alcohols by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 17). Figure 17a represents a type II mechanism. In this mechanism, photoexcited electrons transfer from CB of COF-MT to CB of γ-Fe2O3 and then to CB of MIL101(Fe)-NH₂. As shown in Fig. 17a, the photoexcited electrons in the CB of MIL101(Fe)-NH₂ do not possess sufficient potential to reduce oxygen to superoxide radicals, as their potential is less than the redox potential of O2/O2.− (− 0.33 eV vs. NHE)63. Furthermore, the holes in the VB of COF-MT are unable to oxidize benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde because the oxidation potential of Ph-CH2OH/Ph-CHO (1.98 eV vs. NHE)63 is more positive than the EVB of COF-MT (1.59 eV). Consequently, the conventional type II mechanism fails to align with the experimental results observed for the alcohol oxidation. In contrast, a dual S-scheme mechanism (Fig. 17b) can be proposed for this photocatalytic system in which γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT acts as a ternary heterostructure. In this mechanism, when the ternary heterojunction is irradiated by visible light, γ-Fe2O3, MIL101(Fe)-NH2 and COF-MT are all excited to generate photogenerated electrons and the corresponding h+. Photogenerated electrons transfer from the CB of MOF to the VB of γ-Fe2O3 and then from CB of γ-Fe2O3 to the VB of COF-MT, and recombine with the corresponding h+. As a result, accumulated electrons on the CB of COF-MT with a more negative ECB (− 0.71 eV) than the standard redox potential of O2/O2.− (− 0.33 eV vs. NHE), are able to reduce O2 to O2.−. The EVB of MOF is 3.08 eV, which is more positive than that of Ph-CH2OH/Ph-CHO (1.98 eV vs. NHE), indicating that the h+ on the valence band of MOF can oxidize alcohols to aldehydes. The produced superoxide radicals from oxygen by the electrons on the CB of COF-MT, can also convert the alcohols to aldehydes. The electron-hole transfer between the components of the photocatalyst through a dual S-scheme pathway made γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT acting as a ternary heterostructure. Dual S-scheme pathway decreases the electron–hole recombination rate and increases photocatalytic efficiency. Therefore, γ-Fe2O3/MOF/COF as a ternary photocatalyst exhibited more efficient catalytic activity for the oxidation of alcohols selectively to aldehydes, compared to the only reported MOF/COF photocatalyst in the literature, in which the photo-oxidation was proceeded via a type II pathway by a binary photocatalyst9.

caption.p: Proposed mechanisms for the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT: (a) type II and (b) dual S-scheme.

sec.p: To end, some green metrics65 such as atom economy (AE), atom efficiency (AEf), carbon efficiency (CE), reaction mass efficiency (RME), and optimum efficiency (OE) were calculated to estimate the greenness of the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (Fig. 18). As it is shown in Fig. 18, the high amounts of these green metrics for the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol, 4-nitro- and 4-metoxybenzyl alcohols (Table 2, entries 1, 5 and 7), showed well the greenness of the process.

caption.p: Green metrics including AE, AEf, CE, RME, OE for the photo-oxidation of benzyl alcohol derivatives to benzaldehyde catalyzed by γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT (entries 1, 5 and 7 in Table 2).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, this study presents the design, synthesis, characterization and application of a novel nanomagnetic iron oxide/MOF/COF hybrid material denoted as γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT. The synthesized γ-Fe2O3/MIL101(Fe)-NH2/COF-MT was successfully applied as a dual S-scheme ternary heterostructure photocatalyst for the efficient and selective oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes by air, under sunlight irradiation in ethanol. The unique properties of the catalyst, such as improved light absorption, charge separation, and ease of the catalyst recovery by an external magnet (able to perform seven batches without degradation), using a small amount of the catalyst, sunlight irradiation, air as a safe and plentiful oxidant and ethanol as a green solvent, position it as a promising candidate for the synthesis of aldehydes as fine chemicals. Based on our knowledge, it is the first report on the photo-oxidation of alcohols catalyzed by a nanomagnetic iron oxide/MOF/COF hybrid material.
